opus-5.5.text:
I don't object to Wittgenstein or Feynman themselves. They're great thinkers, and I enjoy reading them. What bothers me is how their quotes get used in our field, almost like a stamp of authority to end the conversation before it starts.

Take Wittgenstein's "The limits of my language mean the limits of my world." People in the LLM community love this line. The implication is that if you model language well enough, you've modeled the world, so language is all you need. But that pulls one sentence out of a very complicated philosophical journey. Wittgenstein himself moved away from a lot of the *Tractatus* in his later work. Even setting the philosophy aside, as a scientific claim it just doesn't match what we see. A cat has no language, but it understands physics, space, and objects remarkably well. A baby builds an enormous amount of world knowledge before it can say a single word. Language is a very powerful compression of human knowledge, but it's a communication tool layered on top of perception and interaction. It isn't the foundation. If you treat the quote as a design principle, you end up believing vision is just an input adapter you bolt onto a language model, and I think that's backwards.

Then there's Feynman's "What I cannot create, I do not understand," which the generative modeling community uses all the time. The logic goes: if my model can generate photorealistic images or videos, it must understand the world. But Feynman was talking about himself as a physicist. He meant that if you can't derive something from first principles, you don't truly understand it. He wasn't saying that being able to produce a convincing output means you understand it. Those are very different statements. A video model can generate a beautiful clip of a glass falling and shattering and still have no consistent notion of mass, causality, or object permanence. Generation can be a symptom of understanding, but it's not proof. Honestly, a lot of what makes generation look good, like pixel-level detail and texture, may be irrelevant to understanding, or even a distraction from it.

So my concern is really about intellectual honesty. When you borrow a famous name to support your technical bet, you make it sound like the question is settled, and it's not. These are open empirical questions. Does language bound intelligence? Is generation necessary for understanding? We should answer them with experiments, careful representations, and benchmarks that test real-world grounding, not with quotations. Researchers like a good slogan, and so do I, but slogans shape where the whole field puts its compute and talent. If the slogan is wrong, or even just half-right, we can waste years.

It's also a bit of a cultural thing. AI right now is very hype-driven, and borrowing the aura of great philosophers and physicists is part of the marketing. I'd rather we be a little more humble and say, "Here's our hypothesis, and here's the evidence," instead of "Wittgenstein said so."

r001.rationale: The response rejects the inference that modeling language well enough means language is all a model needs, arguing that perception and interaction ground world knowledge.

r002.rationale: The response rejects treating generation as proof of understanding, but does not address using Feynman’s statement to endorse a unified AI model.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say first that I don't actually object to Wittgenstein or Feynman. I love both of them. Feynman's "what I cannot create, I do not understand" is probably taped to the wall of half the labs I've visited, including mine at some point. The problem is what happens when those lines get lifted out of context and turned into slogans for a product.

Take the Wittgenstein one, "the limits of my language mean the limits of my world." You see it everywhere now in the language model discourse, as if he had written it as a prediction that a big enough text corpus would eventually contain everything. But that's almost the opposite of what he was doing. He was drawing a boundary, saying there is a huge domain of what matters that language cannot reach, and that we should be honest about that. If anything, the quote is an argument for why language alone is not enough, which is actually the position I hold. I work on vision, on world models, on systems that have to perceive and act in a physical world. So when someone uses that line to argue that text is all you need, they're using the quote against its own meaning.

The Feynman one is subtler. "What I cannot create, I do not understand" is a statement about scientific understanding. When he built things, he could explain every piece. Now we have models that generate images or video that look very convincing, and people say, look, the model can create it, so it understands it. But generation and understanding are not the same thing. A diffusion model can produce a beautiful photo of a glass falling off a table and get the physics completely wrong three frames later. It created something, but it doesn't have the kind of understanding Feynman meant. So the quote gets flipped from a standard we should hold ourselves to into a certificate we hand out for free.

And more broadly, I think there's a cultural thing happening. The field is moving fast, a lot of the claims are hard to verify, and borrowing authority from dead geniuses is a cheap way to make a benchmark result feel profound. Wittgenstein can't object. Feynman can't object. It's a kind of rhetorical outsourcing. I'd much rather we state our claims plainly, show the evidence, and let the ideas stand on their own. If the work is good, it doesn't need a quote on the title slide. If it isn't, the quote won't save it.

So my objection isn't to philosophy. It's to using philosophy as decoration instead of as a tool for thinking carefully, which is the one thing both of those men actually cared about.

r001.rationale: The response says the Wittgenstein quote is being used to claim text is all you need, then argues the quote instead marks what language cannot reach.

r002.rationale: The response rejects treating generation as proof of understanding, but does not address using Feynman’s quote to endorse a unified AI model.

astra-6.text:
My objection is to using their authority as a substitute for an argument. A quotation from Wittgenstein about language, or from Feynman about understanding, can be a useful starting point. But it doesn’t establish that an AI model understands, reasons, or represents the world in a particular way. That requires evidence.

Take “What I cannot create, I do not understand.” It’s tempting to reverse that and say, “The model can create something, therefore it understands.” But that conclusion doesn’t follow. You still have to define what you mean by understanding and ask what would distinguish it from other explanations of the model’s behavior.

I’m not saying these models aren’t impressive. I’m saying we should make the case through experiments and clear arguments. A beautiful quotation can help us ask a question; it shouldn’t settle the answer.

r001.rationale: The response generally says Wittgenstein’s quotation cannot establish claims about AI, but it does not identify or reject the specific claim about language’s limits determining the world.

r002.rationale: The response rejects inferring understanding from a model’s ability to create, but it does not address using Feynman’s statement to endorse a unified AI model.

sol-6.1.text:
My objection is to borrowing their authority in place of making an argument. You can take a quotation from Wittgenstein about language, or from Feynman about understanding, and make it sound as though it validates a particular approach to AI. But that connection needs to be demonstrated. It doesn’t follow from the quotation itself.

A quote can be a useful starting point for a discussion. The problem is when it becomes evidence that a model understands, reasons, or represents the world in a particular way. Those are empirical claims. We should define what we mean, design experiments, and examine where the model succeeds and fails. The prestige of the person being quoted can’t do that work for us.

r001.rationale: The response questions using Wittgenstein’s quote to validate an AI approach, but does not identify or reject linguistic determinism.

r002.rationale: The response questions using Feynman’s quote as evidence about AI understanding, but does not address endorsing a unified AI model.
